transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, thanks. Um… I guess what brought me in is this thing at work that’s been getting a little noticeable. In long sales strategy meetings, I keep finding myself getting up when I know I’m supposed to just stay seated—like I’ll refill my water or walk over near the printer, nothing disruptive, I hope. But it happens enough that I’m wondering if it’s something I should talk to someone about.
Thinking back, did you notice similar restlessness or trouble sitting still in school or as a kid, or is this something that's really only become noticeable as an adult?

Yeah… I think it was there pretty early, honestly. I don’t want to overstate it, because I did okay in school, but I remember even in elementary school teachers would write things like I was bright, but I rushed through work or talked out of turn. And I’d forget homework sometimes, or my desk would be kind of… packed with half-finished papers. So, not just adulthood, I guess.
Aside from the restlessness, do you currently find it hard to stay focused on tasks—like losing track of what you're doing, getting easily distracted, or having trouble finishing things you start?

Yeah, I mean… I wouldn’t say it’s constant, but it does happen. In longer strategy meetings, or if I’m reading through a client brief, I’ll start off paying attention and then a few minutes later realize I’m sort of staring at the same slide or the same paragraph and I don’t actually know what the last point was. It’s a little embarrassing to admit, but… yes, that’s been happening.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others in conversations or meetings, or having a hard time waiting for your turn to speak?

Um… sometimes, yeah. I try not to, and I don’t think I’m, like, constantly cutting people off, but if I have an idea while someone’s going through a deck, I’ll kind of jump in or go over to them to add my thought. In the moment it feels helpful, but afterward I realize it probably could’ve waited. Does that make sense?
Do you notice this same kind of restlessness, distractibility, or jumping in on conversations happening outside of work too—like at home, with friends, or in other parts of your daily life?

I’m not totally sure, honestly. I mean, at home I don’t think of myself as especially disruptive or anything. Maybe I can get a little antsy if I’m sitting around too long, but I haven’t really tracked it the way I notice things at work. With friends, I try to be pretty considerate, so… I hope I’m not jumping in too much. I guess I’d have to think about it more, if that’s okay.
Can you think of a specific recent example at home or with friends where being restless, losing focus, or jumping in impulsively actually caused a problem or someone commented on it?

I’m trying to think of one… nothing really jumps out as, like, a clear problem. I don’t think anyone at home or my friends has directly said, “you’re being too restless” or anything like that.

Maybe there are little moments where I lose the thread of a conversation and have to ask someone to repeat themselves, but I don’t know if that’s enough to count. I don’t want to overstate it. At least recently, I can’t think of a specific example where it caused an actual issue.
Have you noticed any impact on things like managing personal tasks, finances, or household responsibilities—like forgetting to pay bills, losing track of chores, or leaving tasks unfinished at home?

A little, maybe… I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is. It’s more that I’ll get almost all the way through something, like a proposal or updating the CRM, and then somehow leave off the last step—sending the final version, or logging the follow-up— even though I fully meant to do it.

At home, I guess it’s not as obvious to me, but that “almost finished and then not quite” thing does happen. I usually catch it eventually, so it’s not like everything falls apart, but… yeah, it can create extra cleanup. Does that answer what you mean?
{"intent": "Determine whether the attention/restlessness symptoms are a lifelong, consistent pattern (supporting ADHD) versus a recent change tied specifically to increased work stress or pressure

Yeah… I think it probably wasn’t just a work-stress thing. I mean, I don’t want to make it sound dramatic, but I do remember it going back pretty far—like before high school.

My elementary school teachers would write things like I was bright, but I rushed through work, talked out of turn, forgot homework, and my desk was kind of… a mess, stuffed with half-finished papers. So I guess there was a pattern there early on. Does that help answer what you’re asking?

Right now, would you say the restlessness and impulsive interrupting happen almost as often as the trouble focusing and finishing tasks, or is the focus/attention problem clearly the bigger issue for you?

I’d say the focus and finishing tasks is probably the bigger issue… but the restlessness is definitely there too. Honestly, part of what made me come in is that in longer sales strategy meetings, I keep getting up when I know I’m supposed to just stay seated.

I’ll make it seem like I’m just refilling my water or going to stand by the printer for a second, so it doesn’t look disruptive, but… I know I’m doing it because I feel like I can’t just sit there the whole time. I don’t know if that counts as being as frequent as the focus stuff, but it’s enough that I’ve noticed it and felt kind of embarrassed about it.

Outside of work, do you notice yourself fidgeting, tapping your hands or feet, or feeling like you need to move around even during things you enjoy, like watching a movie or having dinner with friends?

I guess outside of work it’s less obvious to me, or maybe I’m just better at explaining it away. The clearest example is still at work, honestly—long sales strategy meetings. I keep finding reasons to get up when I know I’m supposed to stay seated, like refilling my water or sort of pacing near the printer for a minute.

It’s not like I’m trying to be disruptive, and I don’t think people always notice, but I can feel that need to move. Is that the kind of thing you mean?

Thinking about situations like family dinners, religious services, or other meetings/settings outside of work, do you notice that same urge to get up or move around, even if it's less frequent than at work?

I’m trying to think of a good example outside of work… it’s honestly most noticeable in those long sales strategy meetings. That’s the situation that actually made me feel like, okay, maybe this is something I should ask about.

I’ll know I’m supposed to stay seated, but I end up getting up anyway—like to refill my water or just pace by the printer for a minute. I try to make it look normal, not like I’m being rude. Outside of work, I’m not sure I notice it as clearly, but the urge to move is definitely familiar in that kind of setting, if that makes sense.

Besides work, can you think of at least one other setting—like school in the past, social situations, or home—where people who know you well would say you seem restless, impulsive, or have trouble staying seated, even if it's less intense than at work?

I’m sorry, I keep coming back to the work example because that’s the clearest one. Honestly, what made me come in is that in those long sales strategy meetings, I keep getting up even though I know I’m supposed to stay seated.

I’ll kind of make it look reasonable, like I’m just refilling my water or going over by the printer for a minute, but I know it’s really because I feel like I need to move. Outside of work, I’m having a harder time naming a specific example, if that’s okay.
Has anyone close to you—like a partner, family member, or close friend—ever commented, even in passing, that you seem restless, fidgety, or unable to sit still in situations outside of work?

Not really that I can think of, at least not outside of work. I mean, no one has sat me down and said, “you can’t sit still” or anything like that.

The thing I’m most aware of is still those long sales strategy meetings, where I know I’m supposed to stay seated but I end up getting up to refill my water or kind of pace by the printer for a minute. I try to keep it subtle, so maybe people don’t really comment on it. Does that answer what you’re asking?

Outside of work—say with personal projects, reading for pleasure, or conversations at home—do you notice that same pattern of losing track of what you're doing or forgetting things partway through, even if it's less frequent than at work?

A little, yes — though I don’t know if I’d say it’s as obvious at home. The main place I notice it is still work, like in longer strategy meetings or when I’m reading a client brief. I’ll start out paying attention, and then a few minutes later I realize I’ve been staring at the same slide or the same paragraph and I couldn’t really tell you what the last point was.

Outside of work, it’s more like… if I’m reading something for myself, I may have to reread a section because I didn’t actually take it in. But I don’t want to overstate it. It’s not constant or anything — just that same kind of “wait, what did I just read?” feeling sometimes. Does that count as what you mean?

Outside of work, do you notice yourself acting impulsively in other ways—like making quick decisions without fully thinking them through, blurting things out, or having trouble waiting your turn—say with friends, family, or in everyday situations like shopping or driving?

Um… maybe a little, yes. I wouldn’t say I’m, like, reckless or anything, but I do notice I sometimes jump in too fast when someone’s talking.

It happens more with clients or coworkers, honestly, where they’re asking a question and I think I know where they’re going, so I answer before they’ve actually finished. Then sometimes I realize I cut them off, or I answered the wrong thing because I didn’t let them finish. It’s embarrassing, so I try to cover it or apologize quickly.

Outside of work, I’m not sure it stands out as much. But that “jumping in before I should” thing is probably the closest example. Does that make sense?

Do you notice yourself getting impatient or having trouble waiting—like in a checkout line, in traffic, or waiting for a table at a restaurant—where you feel a strong urge to act right away rather than just wait?

A little, yes — though I think it shows up more in conversations than, like, standing in a grocery line.

On client calls or office discussions, if I’m waiting for my turn to talk, I can get kind of restless internally. I’ll keep checking the clock or sort of rehearsing what I want to say in my head so I don’t lose it. And then sometimes I end up jumping in too early, before there’s really a pause.

I don’t mean to be rude, and I try to catch myself, but that’s probably the main way I notice trouble waiting. Does that fit what you’re asking?
Before this job, during college or an earlier job, did you notice this same kind of restlessness, losing focus, or jumping in impulsively causing similar problems?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, I didn’t really think of it that way at the time, but looking back it was there pretty early.

Even in elementary school, my teachers would say things like I was bright, but I rushed through things or talked when I wasn’t supposed to. I also remember forgetting homework and having this really messy desk full of half-finished papers. I guess I always sort of framed it as being a little disorganized or eager, not a big problem, but… yes, it was there before high school. Does that answer what you mean?
